headings.title: Introduction to ICT-Related Addictions in Adolescents
headings.content: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) addictions refer to problematic, compulsive use of digital devices, internet platforms, and virtual environments that interferes with daily functioning. While modern technology forms an essential part of education and socialization in Nigeria and globally, excessive engagement can cross the line from heavy use into behavioral addiction. Adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to ongoing maturation of the prefrontal cortex, which governs impulse control, long-term planning, and emotional regulation. Unlike substance-related disorders, digital addictions involve no chemical ingestion, yet they trigger similar neurochemical reward pathways in the brain. Recognizing this shift requires understanding that a device or platform acts as the delivery mechanism for a constant stream of behavioral reinforcement.

headings.title: Types and Manifestations of Digital Addictions
headings.content:
Digital addiction is a broad umbrella encompassing several distinct behavioral patterns. Clinicians categorize these manifestations based on the specific medium or activity driving the compulsive behavior.

- **Social Media Addiction**: Excessive scrolling, posting, and seeking validation through likes and comments on platforms like Instagram, TikTok, or WhatsApp, leading to severe anxiety when offline.
- **Internet Gaming Disorder**: Uncontrollable engagement in multiplayer online or offline video games, often displacing sleep, schoolwork, and face-to-face social interactions.
- **Cybersex and Pornography Addiction**: Compulsive viewing of digital sexual content or engaging in online sexual chat rooms, impairing real-world interpersonal relationships.
- **Information Overload and Browsing**: Compulsive searching, reading, or collecting of digital data, driven by a fear of missing out (FOMO) or an inability to stop consuming trivia and news.

headings.title: Underlying Psychological and Neurological Factors
headings.content: The addictive pull of modern technology is engineered into software design. Variable reinforcement schedules—such as unpredictable notifications, likes, and loot boxes—trigger the release of dopamine in the brain's mesolimbic pathway, mirroring the mechanisms of slot machines. Beyond neurochemistry, psychological vulnerabilities often set the stage. Adolescents experiencing low self-esteem, social anxiety, depression, or loneliness frequently turn to virtual worlds as a safe, controlled escape from real-world distress. In digital spaces, they can curate identities and find immediate validation that may be lacking in their physical environments. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where emotional distress drives screen use, and subsequent social isolation deepens the underlying depression.

headings.title: Physical and Mental Health Consequences
headings.content: Prolonged and compulsive ICT use exerts a heavy toll on the developing body and mind. Physically, adolescents frequently present with chronic musculoskeletal strain, including text neck, carpal tunnel syndrome, and lower back pain from poor posture during long sitting sessions. Ocular strain, dry eyes, and disrupted circadian rhythms from evening blue light exposure lead to severe sleep deprivation, which compromises immune function and academic performance. Mentally, excessive screen time correlates with heightened rates of anxiety, depressive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, and academic decline. In severe cases, withdrawal from screens triggers intense irritability, agitation, and somatic complaints such as headaches and nausea.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Screening Tools for Youth
headings.content:
Detecting ICT addiction requires a systematic approach during routine adolescent health checks in schools, primary care clinics, or pediatric wards. Because youth rarely present complaining directly of screen addiction, nurses must screen for secondary red flags: sudden drops in academic grades, withdrawal from family activities, chronic fatigue, and intense anger when devices are restricted. Standardized screening instruments help quantify the problem.

| Tool | Focus Area | Target Population |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Young Internet Addiction Test (IAT)** | General compulsive internet use and functional impairment | Adolescents and adults |
| **Problematic and Risky Internet Use Screening Scale (PRIUSS)** | Behavioral, emotional, and cognitive symptoms of overuse | Children and adolescents |
| **Social Media Disorder Scale** | Specific addictive behaviors related to networking platforms | Teens and young adults |

headings.title: Prevention Strategies and Digital Hygiene
headings.content: Preventing digital addiction centers on cultivating healthy boundaries before compulsive patterns become entrenched. Digital hygiene refers to practices that promote safe, balanced, and intentional technology use. Nurses play a vital educational role by guiding parents and adolescents to establish clear device-free zones, such as keeping smartphones out of bedrooms during sleeping hours to protect circadian health. Setting explicit daily time limits for non-academic screen use and encouraging offline hobbies—like sports, arts, or community clubs—helps build a diversified lifestyle. Furthermore, adults must model balanced technology habits, as children frequently mimic the screen behaviors they observe at home.

headings.title: Management, Counseling, and Rehabilitation Approaches
headings.content: When digital addiction causes severe impairment, structured therapeutic intervention is necessary. Management plans rarely involve total abstinence, as technology remains mandatory for modern education and work; instead, the goal is controlled, purposeful use. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) serves as the frontline psychological treatment, helping adolescents identify cognitive distortions, challenge the urge to escape into screens, and develop healthier coping mechanisms for stress. Motivational interviewing assists youth in recognizing the discrepancy between their personal goals and their current screen habits. For severe cases involving comorbid depression or profound withdrawal distress, psychiatric collaboration and family counseling are integrated into the rehabilitation plan to repair interpersonal dynamics.
